chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
title: The Gay Floyd band from Little Rock
summary: He praises an overlooked Arkansas band with a five-man reed section, a sleeper bus, writer Riley Hampton and entertainer Cleophus Jackson.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Oh, a band that really impressed me, and nobody never, ever mentions this band... A band that came from Little Rock, Arkansas -- Gay(?) Floyd. They had a fantastic band. They had a five-man reed section. They had the two tenors, alto and the baritone. They had full brass, a full band. They had a sleeper bus; you know, the first sleeper I saw, where you could sleep in the bus, you know. And they had a whole slew of writers. Practically most of the horn players could write. The one I really remember is

R.O.C. Hampton, Riley Hampton, who did a lot of string work for Chess Records through the years; you know, a lot of Chess big hits. He did the writing for them, you know. But that's one of the first bands I heard where they really were voicing the music really big; you know, they had that big sound. And I used to hear them play...

They had a...oh, a great player... The piano player was fantastic. They used to call him "Screw-Loose"; he was kind of strange, you know. But he could play, and he was fooling with way-out harmonies back in those days, you know. He was somewhere else with the harmonies on this piano, you know.

In those days, the big bands had an entertainer... In fact, Doc Palmer's band had an entertainer who sang and directed the band. His name was Alex McKinney, and he used to try to imitate Cab Calloway -- we used to call him Cab. But he'd sing... We didn't have a microphone; you know, he'd sing through the megaphone during those days.

But getting back to the other band... They had a guy who was an entertainer. This man was so spectacular, named Cleophus Jackson. The Gay(?) Floyd Orchestra... This guy was spectacular. He knew all the arrangements, everything. And the movements that he made were classic, before this... He was a whole production himself, you know.

Yeah, just movements with his body and how he kept the tempo going, and he knew where all the licks was, the little things -- and it was very clever. You know, he wasn't really dancing, but he had these movements that he would keep going, you know. And he was really conducting this band; really conducting this band. He knew every part of every arrangements, and everything... And he did it where it looked beautiful, with finesse, you know. He was classy. Too bad he wasn't put on film in front of this band at some time, you know, during his career.

The only thing I ever heard of him was down through Louisiana, Mississippi, down through Arkansas -- down through that way, you know. But they really had some band. Yeah. And I heard, oh, so many bands that came through.
